spec.cue: Three kinds of colour sensor in many species, a sharp middle, and a view that is less sharp at the edge.

cpd.note: a rounded pick inside the measured span for the group

fovea.note: the app's choice of a sharp middle; records describe a fovea but give no size of sharp centre

fov.note: no whole-field measure was found for these animals; the value is a person's

gain.note: no dim-light measure was found for these animals

rows: Many monkeys and apes have three kinds of colour sensor, with peaks near 430, 539 and 561 nanometres. Some New World monkeys have only two, and the owl monkey has one, so it sees no colour. We show colours the way a person with three kinds of sensor would see them.

A marmoset's fovea is estimated to resolve about 30 cycles per degree, and a rhesus monkey reached 26.3 cycles per degree on a test. Most monkeys and apes are sharper than a person at the centre. We blur the picture to about 10, which is the middle of the measured figures.

Monkeys show direction selectivity in most of the cells of area MT, and 86% of marmoset MT cells respond to the direction of motion. Movement is a strong part of what they see, so the view stresses it.

The width of the sharp middle, the field of view, the gain and the blur at the edge are the app's own picks. No record gives them for these animals, so they are guesses that a person can change in the tuning panel.
Owl monkeys and bushbabies are active at night, and their retinas are built for dim light. Most other monkeys and apes are day-active.

claims.how: The value 10 lies between the marmoset's 30 cycles per degree estimate and the rhesus monkey's 26.3 cycles per degree test ceiling, but is set lower by the app as a rounded pick.

the majority of neurons (80–90%) show clear direction selectivity
Analysis of single units revealed that 86% of cells in area MT show a strong selectivity for the direction of motion of visual stimuli.

rows: A scorpion has one pair of median eyes in the middle of its shield and three to five pairs of smaller lateral eyes at the front corners. In some species the last two pairs of lateral eyes are tiny.
Scorpions are reported to see 360 degrees around the body, with a small overlap of about 40 degrees above the animal where the two median eyes look at the same place.

Both sets of eyes are most sensitive to green light near 500 nm. The lateral eyes also have a weaker peak in the ultraviolet. This view shows one green-sensitive pigment, so the world has a single hue.

Scorpion eyes respond to starlight levels of light, which suits an animal that hides by day and hunts at night. In one desert species the median eyes are about 3 log units more sensitive at night than by day.
The median eyes are thought to give the better picture, with fairly good detail. The lateral eyes may detect only changes in light.

No one has measured how much detail a scorpion sees. This view assumes a coarse picture and a brighter night than a person would see. The squeeze of the whole circle into the screen is the app's choice.
A scorpion finds prey by feeling vibrations in the sand through its legs, up to about 50 cm away, and it tastes the ground with its comb-like pectines. The camera records neither.

claims.how: Both records state a 360 degree field of view for scorpions.
The matrix is built from the single pigment peak of about 500 nm that R6 gives for both sets of eyes.
The matrix is built from one pigment peak at 500 nm, the value R6 gives for both sets of eyes; the mapping to colour is the app's choice.
The one pigment peak is 500 nm, the value R6 gives.

Both sets of eyes are most sensitive to green light (~ 500 nm)

rows: The two big front eyes see only a small patch, but they see it sharply. A typical jumping spider resolves about 3.8 cycles per degree there, and Portia reaches about 12.5, which is close to a bird.
A view all the way round
Three more pairs of small eyes are spaced around the head and together cover almost the whole circle. Their picture is soft, between 0.3 and 1.3 cycles per degree.
The front eyes carry an ultraviolet pigment near 370 nm and a green pigment near 530 nm. Colour is built from those two, so reds and greens run together and ultraviolet counts as a colour of its own.
Still things vanish at the sides
The side eyes behave as though completely blind to stationary objects. A light that only goes on and off draws no turn, and a target that moves does. They are also described as seeing without colour.

The retinas behind the front lenses sweep side to side across what they inspect with a period of 1 to 2 seconds. They also twist about 20 to 30 degrees each way, holding each extreme for several seconds.

The size and position of the sharp patch, the ring where the side eyes take over, the blue channel standing in for ultraviolet, the whole picture's sharpness drawn from a range, the grey sides and the drawing styles are the app's choices.

rows: Whales, dolphins and seals have only one kind of cone or none, so they see little colour. Most of their seeing is done by rod cells, which give a picture of light and dark. A blue-green tint is the closest a phone can show.

A humpback whale resolves about 3.3 cycles per degree and a Bryde's whale about 4.8. Toothed whales and harbour seals reach about 2.6 to 11.5. We blur the picture to about 3.3, which is a tenth of your sharpness or less.
Dolphins see a panoramic field of 120 to 130 degrees, and the two eyes overlap only 20 to 30 degrees. We widen the picture to 130 degrees.

The colour tint, the gate that fades still things, the gain, the glow of the reflecting layer and the saturation are the app's own choices, since the records give no figures for them. A reflecting layer is recorded in several cetaceans, so the app draws a sheen with its strength chosen by the app.

claims.how: The value 3.3 sits between the cited acuity records for toothed whales and porpoises (2.6 to 3.3) and the humpback whale (3.3), so it is a middle value of those records.
The value 130 is the upper end of the 120 to 130 degree panoramic field given for dolphins.

Scorpion eyes peak in the green near 500 to 570 nanometres and have a secondary peak in the ultraviolet, so the picture leans toward green and ultraviolet light.
Scorpion eyes respond to starlight levels of light, so the view keeps a bright picture on a moonless night.

No one has measured how sharp a scorpion's picture is. This view keeps a coarse picture of shapes, with colour limited to green, blue and ultraviolet, and the brightness and fading are the app's choices.
Scorpions sense vibration through slits in their legs and touch through hairs and pegs. Most of what they find comes through these senses, which the picture does not show.

rows: An octopus resolves about 12 cycles per degree in one test and a squid about 6.6. A cuttlefish is put at about 8. A person manages about 30, so the screen is blurred to 8 cycles per degree.

Octopus, squid and cuttlefish carry one visual pigment, and tests find no colour vision. Octopus pigments peak between 475 and 487 nanometres. The picture keeps brightness weighted toward blue-green light and loses hue.

A cuttlefish eye covers 253 degrees on the horizontal plane, and a growing oval squid covers 295 to 329 degrees. A cuttlefish can overlap its two eyes in front by 86 degrees. The picture uses 291 degrees, the middle of 253 and 329.
An octopus pupil is round in darkness and narrows to a horizontal slit in bright light.
An octopus retina packs about 55,000 cells per square millimetre into a central horizontal stripe, against 18,000 to 22,000 at the edges. Cuttlefish and squid also have a streak or a centred area.
No reflective layer behind the retina has been found in any squid studied, and none in any cephalopod to date. The picture carries no sheen.
Octopuses tell vertical from horizontal polarized light, and two species respond to differences of about 1.3 degrees in its angle. The picture leaves it out for now.

The one figure of 8 cycles per degree for the whole group, the 291 degree field, the horizontal slit for every animal, the one-pigment colour mapping, the absence of sheen and the weights of the sharp stripe are the app's own settings. Squid and cuttlefish pupils are not described in the records, so the octopus slit stands for them.

rows: A bee sees much less detail than a person. The best measured limit is about a quarter of a grating cycle per degree, so the view is soft everywhere.
A bee sees nearly all round itself, with a small blind patch behind and below. This view squeezes a wide field into the phone.

Bees have three kinds of colour receptor, peaking in the ultraviolet, blue and green. Phone cameras capture little ultraviolet, so the view shows it as blue, and the colours shift toward the long end of the spectrum.

The soft glow on movement, the colour of that glow, the blank sharpness shape, the squeeze of the field and the lack of depth blur are the app's own choices, since no record gives values for how a bee's movement looks on screen.

R35 gives a field of view of about 300 degrees horizontally for bees; it is a general figure for bees, so the grade is g.
The BEE matrix uses peaks 346, 430 and 540 nm, taken from the Apis mellifera worker entry of the Apidae compilation (R43, R73 and R85 give 346, 430 and 540), with the false colour convention of R268.

spec.cue: Three kinds of colour sensor and a picture nearly as sharp as yours.

cpd.note: a figure between a rhesus monkey's 26.3 and a marmoset's close to 30; the app picks one value to speak for the whole order

M.note: the three-cone case of macaques, baboons, apes and many others; the app's mapping of those peaks

primate_trichromat.note: peaks near 430, 531 and 561 nanometres, as in a macaque

rows: A macaque has three kinds of colour sensor, most sensitive near 430, 531 and 561 nanometres. That is close to your own set, so the colours stay much as you know them.
Owl monkeys have only one kind of cone and lack colour vision. Male marmosets have two kinds. Howler monkeys have three. This view draws the three-cone case.

A rhesus monkey reached 26.3 cycles per degree, and a marmoset's cone mosaic could support close to 30. A person sees about 30, so the picture is only slightly softer. A mouse lemur manages about 4.9, which is far blurrier.
Most monkeys have a fovea, a small pit in the retina where cones are packed closely. Squirrel monkeys show it clearly. Owl monkeys have only a rudimentary one.
Cells in the visual cortex of macaques respond to the small differences between the two eyes' views. Diurnal primates use these differences to judge distance among branches.

One sharpness value stands for all primates, and the app picks it between two measurements. The colour matrix is the app's mapping of three measured peaks onto your screen. The drawing option for colour is also the app's.
